summary: The second vision of wisdom opens the Parables: Enoch the son of Jared lifts his voice to speak words of the Holy One before the Lord of Spirits to those on earth who dwell across ages. The chapter frames the entire Parables booklet as wisdom for men of old and those to come, establishing that what follows is not new law but disclosed holy words. It sets the expectation of judgment and blessing that the three parables will unfold.
whyItMatters: It opens the book of Parables as wisdom from Enoch before the Lord of Spirits — the frame that makes chapters 38–71 read as revealed judgment rather than chronicle, with Jude's later citation in the background.

context.author: The chapter presents itself as Enoch's revealed words — a pseudepigraphal seer voice recalling what angels showed him — while the book as a whole is understood as Jewish apocalyptic composed in Aramaic between the third and first centuries BC and preserved complete in Ge'ez.
context.audience: First addressed to righteous Jews under Hellenistic and then Roman pressure who needed assurance that heavenly judgment outweighs earthly oppression, and later preserved by Ethiopian Christians as canonical scripture for liturgical hearing.
context.date: The Parables (37–71) lack Qumran attestation; many place them late first century BC to early first century AD on grounds of Greek circulation and Roman horizon, though the debate remains — some argue second century BC or late editorial strata.
context.setting: Heaven's court before the Lord of Spirits — visions of wisdom, congregation, mansions, storehouses, and the four presences who do not sleep — with Enoch lifted to hear and see.
context.literaryForm: Parable (mashal) — apocalyptic revelation through vision report, angelic dialogue, heavenly tour, and symbolic inventory of metals, mountains, and valleys; titles like Elect One, Righteous One, and Son of Man accumulate for a single enthroned judge.

keyVerses.text: The second vision which he saw, the vision of wisdom—which Enoch the son of Jared, the son of Mahalalel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, saw.
keyVerses.why: Verse 1 opens the chapter — The second vision which he saw, the vision of wisdom—wh — and is the point the guide returns to when explaining why this scene matters.

keyVerses.text: It were better to declare (them only) to the men of old time, but even from those that come after we will not withhold the beginning of wisdom.
keyVerses.why: This verse carries the middle turn — It were better to declare (them only) to the men o — and clarifies the chapter's contribution to the Parables' judgment arc.

keyVerses.text: Now three Parables were imparted to me, and I lifted up my voice and recounted them to those that dwell on the earth.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse 37:5 seals the movement — Now three Parables were imparted to me, and I lift — showing where the chapter lands.

themes: men of old and those to come

questions.question: What is the "Lord of Spirits" in chapter 37 of 1 Enoch?
questions.answer: It is Enoch's most frequent divine title in the Parables — the Lord who commands spirits, angels, and stars, seated with the Head of Days, weighing actions and naming the Son of Man before creation. The title keeps judgment in view as command over all spirits rather than over armies alone.

questions.question: What is a distinctive phrase in chapter 37 that an English reader might miss?
questions.answer: A repeated title or term — Lord of Spirits, Son of Man, Elect One, Head of Days, or fountain of righteousness — carries more than its English gloss. In this chapter the term recurs as a theological argument about enthronement and judgment, and Charles's brackets ⌈⌉ signal where he restored Ge'ez. The English can vary the wording while the Ge'ez insists on the same name.

questions.question: Which verse in chapter 37 is hardest to read, and why?
questions.answer: Verse 37:1 can feel opaque because its imagery — heavenly court, weighed luminaries, descending children, or a Son of Man before creation — assumes an apocalyptic calendar and divine-council worldview the modern reader does not share. The chapter does not pause to define that background; it shows the court convened and the lot divided, leaving the reader to infer why merely human power is judged from heaven.

questions.question: What does this chapter say about the righteous and sinners?
questions.answer: The chapter holds the two lots together: elect and holy children, righteous mansions, fountain of righteousness that fails not for the holy, and expulsion, barring, and burning valley for sinners, kings, and mighty who denied the dwelling. The division is not sentiment but location — where each is allowed to dwell when judgment comes.

questions.question: How does this chapter relate to Daniel or Genesis?
questions.answer: It draws on Daniel 7 — Head of Days, one like a son of man enthroned — and on Genesis 6's sons-of-God frame, but reworks them as a heavenly liturgy where intercession and weighing precede the valley. The allusion is acknowledged as scriptural echo, not as proof that the two texts describe the same dated event.

questions.question: What does this chapter keep calling its audience to become?
questions.answer: To draw near as elect and righteous who have not denied the Lord of Spirits, whose prayer ascends and whose names are before the Head of Days — not to gather data about stars but to be found among those whom the Elect One chooses and preserves when the valley is prepared.

questions.question: How does this chapter fit inside the Book of Parables?
questions.answer: It belongs to the central Parables (37–71), flanked by the Watchers' fall and the heavenly tours; reading it with 46–48 and 62–63 reveals a single figure under several names — Son of Man, Elect One, Righteous One — seated to judge and vindicate, while 52–54 prepare the valley instrument for that sentence.

questions.question: Where do readers differ about this chapter?
questions.answer: Readers differ on whether its language — Son of Man named before sun and stars, mountains of metal, deep valley with burning fire — points to an imminent Roman-era vindication or to a symbolic pattern about all imperial power. The text's claim that the Elect One will judge the mighty is presented as shared, while timetable and historical referent are debated without staging a winner.

glossary.def: The Parables' chief divine title — the Lord who commands spirits, angels, and stars, weighing actions and enthroning the Son of Man beside the Head of Days.
Personified revelation that found no dwelling among men and returned to heaven, now poured out like water before the Elect One who reveals hidden things.
